_howTo: Edit any "text" freely. Keep "kind", "figure", "goal" and "options" as they are (they wire up the live figures). You can add, remove or reorder text blocks, and add or rename parts. Markup in text: **bold**, *italic*, [[words|colour]] to tie words to a figure colour (parcel = orange rising air, env = violet surrounding air, dew = teal dew point), and [^id] for a footnote. A footnote marker goes straight after the word or sentence it belongs to, with no space, and shows as a small raised number that opens a popup. Its note lives in "footnotes" at the end of the file under the same id, with a "kind" ("technical" for a term or detail, coloured teal, which also goes into the journal's glossary; "digression" for a side trip, coloured rose), a "title" and a "text". Add "glossary": false to keep a technical note out of the glossary, or a term ("glossary": "Radiosonde") to list it under that name. Numbers count up through the lesson by themselves. The lessons tell no story: the radio talks and the locals asking forecast questions (by forecast "id") are in data/radio.
title: Wind shifts, cold fronts, and radar
teaches: How do you track a whole storm from start to finish? The low and its fronts, the barometer, why warm fronts soak and cold fronts squall, reading the wind and the high cloud across it, and what weather radar shows

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: The storms that bring most of our rain are whirls of air a thousand kilometres or more across, called **lows**. A low has a warm front, a warm sector and a cold front, and drifts east at about 30 km (20 miles) an hour.
The **barometer** weighs the air overhead. A steady fall says a low is coming; a sharp rise says its cold front has gone by.
A warm front lifts air gently up a long ramp, so it brings wide layers and long, light rain. A cold front shoves air up a steep nose, so it brings a narrow line of towers and short, hard showers.
With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left. If the high cloud crosses from your left to your right, the weather is getting worse; from right to left, better.
**Weather radar** sees rain, not cloud: a wide green shield for a warm front’s steady rain, a thin red line of cells for a cold front’s squall, magenta for hail.

blocks.text: Lesson 4 followed the cloud of a warm front from the first wisp of cirrus down to the soaking nimbostratus. That front was only one edge of something much bigger. This lesson steps back to see the whole storm, and adds the instruments a forecaster reads alongside the sky: the barometer, the wind vane and the thermometer.
By the end you should be able to watch one sky for two days and say what each cloud in it means, using everything from the first five lessons at once.

Across the middle latitudes, cold air from the north and warm air from the south meet along a long, wavering boundary. Every few days a kink in that boundary grows into a great whirl of air a thousand kilometres or more across. Near its centre the air pressure is lower than all around it, so forecasters call the whole thing a **low**, or a mid-latitude storm.

Air drawn in toward the low does not flow straight to its centre. Because the Earth turns beneath it, air moving across the northern half of the world is steered a little to the right[^coriolis], so the inflowing air spirals in, circling the low anticlockwise as it goes. That turning wind drags warm air north on the low’s eastern side and cold air south on its western side.

Where the warm air advances on cold air, its leading edge is the **warm front**. Where cold air advances on warm air, its edge is the **cold front**. The wedge of warm air between them is the **warm sector**.[^front-name]

blocks.caption: A storm seen from above, as on a weather map. The dashed line is the path a town takes through it as the storm drifts east.

blocks.text: On a weather map the warm front wears red half-moons and the cold front blue triangles, each pointing the way its front is going. The whole whirl drifts east, carried along by the westerly winds high overhead, at something like 30 km an hour.

A town in the storm’s path meets its parts in order, along the dashed line on the map: first the high cloud far ahead of the warm front (1), then the warm front itself, then the warm sector (2), then the cold front and the cold air behind it (3). The barometer is the instrument that tracks it best, so it comes first; then the whole storm going by, the shapes of the two fronts, what the wind says, and what the radar sees.

Air has weight. The column of air standing on each square metre of ground, all the way up to the top of the atmosphere, weighs about ten tonnes. You do not feel it because it presses on you from every side at once, and from inside your body too, so the pushes balance.

In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli found a way to weigh that column. He filled a long glass tube with mercury, a liquid metal fourteen times heavier than water, and stood it upside down in a dish of mercury. The mercury in the tube sank a little and then stopped, about 760 millimetres high, with nothing at all in the space above it.

What holds it up is the air pressing down on the open dish. When the column of air overhead weighs more, it pushes the mercury a little higher; when it weighs less, the mercury sinks. That instrument is a **barometer**.[^puy-de-dome]

blocks.caption: What a barometer weighs: the column of air and the column of mercury weigh the same. The scale beside the tube is magnified.

blocks.text: Forecasters give the pressure in hectopascals, also called millibars: about 1013 at sea level on an average day. American barometers read the height of the mercury in inches, where the same average day is 29.92. A deep storm can drag the pressure down to 980 hectopascals or below; a strong high can push it past 1035.

Why does the pressure fall as a low comes? Near the ground, air spirals in toward the low and rises. That rising air is what makes the storm’s cloud: lifted air cools to its dew point, just as in Lesson 1. Rising air alone would not change the weight, since it is still overhead. But high up, the winds carry it away sideways, out of the column, faster than new air spirals in at the bottom. With less air overhead, the column weighs less, and the barometer falls.

A high is the reverse. Air sinks from above, warming and drying as it is squeezed, so highs bring clear, settled weather. The same sinking air makes the warm lid that flattens heaps into stratocumulus, from Lesson 2.

The number on the barometer matters less than which way it is moving. A barometer that falls steadily, about one hectopascal every three hours, for half a day or more, says a low is on its way. A fall faster than a hectopascal an hour says a strong storm with strong winds. A rise says the storm is going.

That is why a forecaster keeps a **barograph**: a pen on an arm, moved by a sealed metal capsule that swells and shrinks with the pressure, drawing on a paper drum that clockwork turns once a week. One glance shows not only the pressure now but how it has been going.

blocks.caption: A barograph. Its sealed, emptied capsules are squeezed thinner as the pressure rises and spring back as it falls; the lever turns that into the pen rising and falling on a week’s chart.

blocks.text: Now follow a whole storm across a town. The figure is a slice through the storm from west to east, like the warm front in Lesson 4, but long enough to hold the warm front, the warm sector and the cold front together. The storm slides in from the left; the barograph underneath traces the pressure as it goes.

Under the slice, the colder air is shaded blue: under the warm front’s long ramp, and behind the cold front’s steep nose. The town’s wind, temperature and dew point are under the slice, with the barograph below them. Heights are stretched about 100 times, so the gentle ramp looks steep.

blocks.caption: A storm crossing a town, west to east, with the barograph below.
blocks.task: Let the whole storm go by, until the barometer is rising again.

blocks.text: **Ahead of the warm front**, the barometer starts falling about the time the first cirrus appears, and keeps falling steadily as the cloud thickens. The wind shifts from south toward southeast and freshens, because the town lies on the low’s east side, where the air circling the low is also being drawn in toward it.

Once the rain starts, it falls through the cold air under the front. Some of it evaporates on the way down, adding vapour to that air and raising its dew point. Before long the air near the ground reaches its dew point too, and ragged shreds of low cloud (sailors call them **scud**), low stratus or even fog forms beneath the nimbostratus: Lesson 1’s cloud, made a new way.

**In the warm sector**, the warm front goes by and everything changes at once. The wind swings round to the south or southwest, the temperature jumps, and the air feels muggy, because its dew point is high: close to the temperature itself. The barometer stops falling and holds nearly steady. The sky is often a grey, broken deck of stratocumulus or stratus, with the sun breaking through now and then.

**At the cold front**, the barometer reaches its lowest point and then turns sharply upward. A line of towering cumulus and cumulonimbus marches in from the west: a squall: a sudden blast of gusty wind (the **gust front** from Lesson 5, cold air rushing out ahead of the towers), then heavy showers, whose worst seldom lasts more than an hour, sometimes with thunder. The wind swings to the west or northwest, and the temperature and the dew point both drop.

**Behind the cold front**, the sky clears from the west and the air is so clean that distant hills look close. The cold air is now flowing over ground still warm from the warm sector, and air heated from below is unstable, as in Lesson 2: bright, crisp heaps of cumulus pop up, and a few may grow big enough to shower. The barometer keeps rising.

When the wind drops on the first night behind the front, the sky is clear, the air is still and the ground is damp from the rain. That is Lesson 1’s recipe for fog in the hollows, or in autumn for the first frost.

blocks.caption: A warm front and a cold front, drawn to the same scale.

blocks.text: Why is a warm front’s cloud a wide sheet of layers, while a cold front’s cloud is a narrow line of towers? Both fronts lift warm air. The difference is how steeply.

At a warm front, the warm air is doing the pushing. It cannot shove the heavy cold air aside, so it rides up over it on a long, gentle ramp, rising one kilometre for every hundred or more. At a cold front, the cold air is doing the pushing. Dense cold air drives in under the warm air like the blade of a snowplough, and friction with the ground holds back its lowest layer, so its nose is blunt: one in fifty, and as steep as one in thirty near the ground.

How fast the air is lifted is the front’s speed multiplied by its slope. Take a front moving at 30 km an hour (cold fronts often go faster still). That is about 8 metres a second; on a ramp of one in a hundred, the air climbs 8 centimetres a second: a slow crawl. Lifted that gently, the air cools a little at a time over a wide area, and spreads into layers.

On a nose of one in thirty, the same air is shoved up more than three times as fast, straight out of the moist warm sector. It reaches its cloud base, half a kilometre up, in about half an hour instead of nearly two hours, and if it is even slightly unstable, it keeps rising on its own, as cumulus does in Lesson 2. The front sets off towers.

blocks.caption: Warm air carried up the face of a front, drawn as a cold front pushing in from the left. A warm front is the same picture mirrored; what sets the cloud is the slope. Heights are stretched 20 times.
blocks.task: Steepen the front until the lifted air builds towers.

blocks.text: Notice what happens to the rain in the figure. A front lifts about the same amount of water either way, about ten millimetres. A gentle front spreads it over a wide belt, so any one spot gets hours of light, steady rain: the soaking kind that sinks into a field. A steep front squeezes it into a narrow band, so it comes down hard and is over quickly, and much of it runs off.
That is why the warm front’s rain is called **steady** and the cold front’s rain is called **showers**, and why a forecaster can tell which front is coming from the shape of the cloud alone.

Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts, and in an older storm the cold front can catch up with the warm front ahead of it. The warm sector is then lifted right off the ground, and the two fronts join into an **occluded front**, drawn on maps as a purple line with both half-moons and triangles. Its sky is a mixture: layers with showers hidden inside them. Many Pacific storms are already occluded by the time they reach the Northwest.

blocks.caption: How a storm occludes, seen from above.

blocks.text: In 1857 the Dutch meteorologist Christophorus Buys Ballot wrote down a rule that sailors had half known for centuries. In the northern half of the world, stand with your back to the wind, and low pressure is on your left, a little ahead of you. (South of the equator, it is on your right.)

blocks.caption: Buys Ballot’s rule, from above: back to the wind, and the low is on your left.

blocks.text: Since lows drift from west to east, the wind tells you where the low is, and the way the wind changes tells you where it is going. When a low passes north of you, as most storms crossing the northern United States do, the wind backs a little as the storm approaches, then turns clockwise as it goes by: from southeast, to south and southwest, then west or northwest behind the cold front.

blocks.caption: The wind at one town through a storm, seen from above: A ahead of the warm front, B in the warm sector, C at the cold front, D behind it.

blocks.text: A wind that shifts clockwise (east to south to west) is said to **veer**; one that shifts anticlockwise **backs**. A backing wind with a falling barometer means the weather is getting worse. A veering wind with a rising barometer means it is getting better.

The high cloud gives you a second wind vane. Up at cirrus height the wind blows from a different direction than at the ground, steered by where the warm and cold air lie, and ahead of a low it carries the cloud across from the west.

The **crossed-winds rule** turns that into a quick test. Stand with your back to the wind at the ground and watch the high cloud. If it is moving across from your left, a low is approaching and the weather will get worse. If it comes from your right, the low is moving away and the weather will improve. If it moves straight toward you or away from you, along the same line as the surface wind, expect little change for now.

blocks.caption: The crossed-winds rule, for the northern half of the world.

blocks.text: Like every rule of thumb, it needs a real sky to work on: watch the highest cloud you can see, not low scud, which moves with the surface wind. And it is best used with the barometer and the clouds’ own sequence, not instead of them.

parts.title: Seeing inside the storm: weather radar

blocks.text: Everything so far you can do with your eyes, a barometer and a wind vane. Since the Second World War, forecasters have had one more instrument that sees inside the storm itself, and today anyone with a radar map on a telephone has it too. It is worth learning to read.

Forecasters can watch this happen with **weather radar**. A radar dish sends out short pulses of microwaves, about ten centimetres long, and listens for the faint echo that comes back when a pulse hits something. The time the echo takes to return gives the distance, and the way the dish is pointing gives the direction. Turning round and round, it maps every shower within a couple of hundred kilometres. Radar was built during the Second World War to find aircraft, and its operators soon found their screens cluttered with rain.

blocks.caption: A radar pulse sent into a cubic metre of air holding half a gram of water, as cloud droplets or as rain.
blocks.task: Make the drops big enough for the radar to see them as rain.

blocks.text: Each drop sends back an echo that grows with the sixth power of its width: a drop twice as wide echoes 64 times as strongly. Shared out into drops twice as wide, the same water makes only an eighth as many, so the echo still grows eightfold. That is why radar sees rain and not cloud: cloud droplets are about a hundred times narrower than raindrops, and even a thick cloud barely registers. The echo is measured in **dBZ**, a scale on which every 10 points means ten times stronger. Light rain shows at about 20, a downpour at 50, and hail above 60. Ice sends back only about a fifth of the echo the same water would.

Most rain from deep cloud starts out as snow high up and melts on the way down (Lesson 7 shows why), and the melting shows up on radar as a stripe. Above the freezing level the snowflakes are big, but they are ice, so they echo weakly. Just below it they start to melt: still as big as snowflakes, but coated in water, they echo like enormous raindrops. A few hundred metres lower they have melted through and collapsed into raindrops, smaller and falling about five times faster, so they are spread more thinly and the echo drops again. The result is the **bright band**, a level stripe of strong echo just under the 0 °C line, and a forecaster can read the height of the freezing level straight off it.

blocks.caption: A slice through steady rain from a layer cloud, as a radar scanning up and down sees it. On the right, the echo by height.
blocks.task: Lower the freezing level until snow reaches the ground.

blocks.text: On a winter day the freezing level can come right down to the fields, and the band comes down with it. A bright band sinking lower and lower through a storm tells a forecaster the rain is about to turn to snow.

Weather radar shows the difference at a glance, and it is the quickest way to tell the two fronts apart. Ahead of the warm front lies a wide shield of blue and green: steady rain, hundreds of kilometres across. Along the cold front runs a thin line of yellow and red, sometimes magenta: cells of heavy rain and hail with dry gaps between them. Behind the cold front, small showers pop up here and there over the warm ground, and the warm sector between the fronts is mostly dry.

blocks.caption: The storm from the start of the lesson, as a radar map shows it.

blocks.text: The front’s steepness is what sorts the rain this way. About the same water falls either way. A gentle ramp spreads it evenly over a wide band; a steep nose crams it into a few towers, each pouring down far harder than the steady rain, while the air between them stays dry.

blocks.caption: The front from the steepness figure, seen from above as on a radar screen. Its rain falls behind its nose.
blocks.task: Steepen the front until its rain breaks up into cells.

blocks.text: So when the radar shows a wide, smooth field of green spreading in from the west, expect a long, steady soaking. When it shows a thin, ragged line of red, expect a short downpour, a gust of wind and a sharp change in the weather as it goes by.

Radar shows the same life from outside. The first echo appears high in the growing tower, five or six kilometres up where ice and supercooled water meet, often ten to twenty minutes before any rain reaches the ground. In the mature stage the core reaches from the ground far up into the cloud, at 50 dBZ and more, and hail shows as a magenta heart in the middle of it. The anvil, made of small ice crystals, barely registers. At the end the echo sinks out of the bottom of the cloud as the last rain falls, and only the faint anvil is left.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell on radar at each stage of its life, sliced through the middle. The white shapes are the cloud; the colours are what the radar sees.

blocks.title: Reading a radar map
points: A wide, smooth shield of green and blue spreading from the west: a warm front’s steady rain. Settle in for hours.
A thin, ragged line of yellow and red: a cold front’s squall line. A short downpour, a gust, and a sharp change behind it.
A small, intense blob with a magenta heart: a thunderstorm cell with hail.
A level stripe of strong echo in the steady rain: the bright band, the freezing level. Sinking toward the ground, it means rain turning to snow.

blocks.text: Here is a storm read the way a forecaster reads it, hour by hour, with every lesson in play. It is an early autumn storm reaching the Columbia Basin.

**Monday dawn.** Fog lies in the low fields after a clear, calm night (Lesson 1), and burns off by mid-morning. A few flat cumulus form, and stay flat under the warm lid of the high that has kept the week fine (Lessons 1 and 2). The barometer reads high and steady.

**Monday afternoon.** Cirrus hooks spread in from the west (Lesson 4). The barometer has started to fall, about one hectopascal every three hours. With your back to a light southeast wind, the cirrus is moving across from your left: a low is coming.
**Monday night.** A ring round the moon: cirrostratus with its 22° halo. The cloud sends the ground’s heat back down, so there is no fog or frost tonight (Lesson 1).

**Tuesday morning.** Altostratus, with the sun a dim disc behind frosted glass and no shadows (Lesson 4), lowering through the morning into grey nimbostratus. East of the mountains the rain is light; Lesson 7 shows why.
**Tuesday afternoon.** The warm front goes by. The wind veers to the southwest, it turns mild and muggy, and the barometer steadies. A broken grey deck of stratocumulus (Lesson 2).

**Tuesday evening.** A dark line of towers in the west, and on the radar a thin red line: the cold front. The gust front, a brief downpour, perhaps thunder: count from flash to bang and divide by three (Lesson 5). The wind swings to the northwest and the barometer jumps.

**Wednesday.** A cold, clear, gusty morning; by midday, crisp cumulus heaps over the hills, set off by cold air over warm ground (Lessons 1 and 2). The barometer keeps climbing. That night the wind drops and the sky stays clear: the first frost.

blocks.title: Reading a storm as it comes
points: First cirrus spreading from the west, barometer starting to fall: a low is coming. Rain within a day or so.
A halo, then altostratus that wipes out shadows: rain within hours. A backing wind and a falling barometer agree, and the radar shows a wide green shield to the west.
The warm front goes by: the wind veers, it turns mild and muggy, the barometer steadies.
A line of towers in the west, a thin red line on the radar, and the barometer turning up: the cold front’s squall. Then clearing, colder, gusty, with heaps.

blocks.text: First name the clouds in the photos. Then read each sky, with its barometer and its wind, and say what is coming.

blocks.caption: A sky, with the barometer and the wind. What is coming?

items.question: Cirrus at noon has spread into a milky veil by evening. The barometer has fallen 3 hPa since noon, and the wind has backed from south to southeast. What is coming?
options: A cold front, with a gusty squall line due within the hour
A warm front, with steady rain likely within a day
A fine, settled spell, as the high cloud drifts on east
items.why: Cirrus thickening into cirrostratus, a steadily falling barometer and a backing wind all say the same thing: the warm front of a low is on its way, and its rain is usually less than a day off.
instruments: Wind: backed from south to southeast

items.question: A squall came through at six with a gust and a downpour. Since then the wind has swung to the northwest and the barometer has risen 4 hPa in three hours. What is tomorrow like?
options: Steady rain all day, as the storm’s warm front comes in behind it
Warm and muggy, with the wind swinging back round to the south
Clear and cooler, gusty, with crisp heaps of cumulus by midday
items.why: The cold front has gone by. Behind it come colder, drier air, a veering wind and a rising barometer; cold air over warm ground sets off bright heaps of cumulus by midday.
instruments: Barometer: up 4 hPa in three hours

items.question: With your back to a south wind, you watch high cirrus moving across the sky from your left to your right. What does the crossed-winds rule say?
options: A low is approaching, so the weather will get worse
The low is moving away, so the weather will get better
No change for now, as the cloud and wind agree
items.why: Back to the surface wind, with the high cloud coming from your left, a low is on its way. The rule needs the highest cloud you can see, not low scud, which moves with the surface wind.

items.question: The radar shows a wide green shield over you that has rained steadily all morning, and behind it, far to the west, a thin line of red and magenta. What is the line?
options: The tail of the same steady rain, thinning out as it ends
The cold front’s squall line, with gusts, downpours and perhaps hail
A warm front, coming to bring a second day of steady rain
items.why: The wide shield is the warm front’s steady rain; the thin, intense line behind it is the cold front’s cells, where the steep nose crams the rain into towers. Red is a downpour, magenta hail.

items.question: Mares’ tails at teatime, a ring round the moon by bedtime, and the barometer down since noon. I want rain on my new-sown winter wheat. Should I drill it tomorrow?
options: No: mares’ tails at teatime mean a dry week ahead
Wait a week: rain this far off won’t reach us soon
Yes: drill it tomorrow, as rain is likely within a day
items.why: Cirrus thickening into a halo-making veil with a falling barometer is the warm front’s cloud arriving. Its rain usually follows within a day: light, steady rain, just the kind that settles new-sown seed.

items.question: The rain stopped at noon. It’s mild and muggy now, the wind is southwest and the barometer has stopped falling. I’m due to fly the mail to Spokane at seven tonight. Any trouble?
options: Yes: the cold front’s squall line is still to come
No: the rain has stopped, so the storm is over
Only fog, late tonight, once the wind dies down
items.why: Mild, muggy air, a southwest wind and a steady barometer after the rain mean the warm front has gone and you are in the warm sector. The cold front, with its line of towers and gusts, is still to come.

learned: Mid-latitude storms are lows a thousand kilometres or more across, with winds circling them anticlockwise (in the northern half of the world); a warm front, a warm sector and a cold front pass a town in order as the storm drifts east at about 30 km (20 miles) an hour.
A barometer weighs the air overhead (about 1013 hPa, or 29.92 inches of mercury, on an average day); a steady fall says a low is coming, and a sharp rise follows its cold front.

The wind backs to the southeast ahead of a warm front, veers to the southwest in the mild, muggy warm sector, and swings to the west or northwest behind the cold front, which brings colder, drier air, clearing skies and crisp cumulus.
A warm front lifts air slowly up a gentle ramp, making wide layers and long, light rain; a cold front shoves air up a steep nose, making a line of towers and short, heavy showers.
With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left; high cloud crossing from your left says the weather will worsen, from your right that it will improve.

Radar sees raindrops, not cloud droplets: a wide green shield is a warm front’s steady rain, a thin red line a cold front’s squall, magenta hail, and a level bright band the melting snow at the freezing level.
next: Next lesson: local tricks. What the mountains and the winter do to the forecast, and the rare skies they make.

lows.title: A storm’s anatomy
lows.text: Mid-latitude storms are lows, whirls of air a thousand kilometres or more across where the pressure is lowest at the centre. Winds circle a low anticlockwise in the northern half of the world, drawing warm air north on its east side and cold air south on its west. The warm front leads, the warm sector follows, and the cold front brings up the rear, as the whole storm drifts east at about 30 km an hour.

barometer.title: The barometer
barometer.text: A barometer weighs the column of air overhead: about ten tonnes on every square metre, enough to hold up 760 mm of mercury (29.92 inches, 1013 hPa). Its trend matters more than its reading. A steady fall of about 1 hPa every three hours says a low is coming; a fall faster than 1 hPa an hour, a strong storm; a sharp rise, the cold front gone by.

cold-front.title: A cold front
cold-front.text: Dense cold air drives in under warm air with a steep, blunt nose, lifting it fast enough to set off a narrow line of towering cumulus and cumulonimbus. It brings a squall of gusts and heavy showers, often in under an hour; the wind swings to the west or northwest, temperature and dew point drop, the barometer jumps, and clear, cold air with crisp cumulus follows.

crossed-winds.title: Reading the wind
crossed-winds.text: Stand with your back to the wind and low pressure is on your left (Buys Ballot’s rule, for the northern half of the world). A wind that backs while the barometer falls means worse weather; one that veers while it rises, better. With your back to the surface wind, high cloud coming from your left says a low is approaching; from your right, that it is moving away.

coriolis.title: Coriolis effect
coriolis.text: This steering is the **Coriolis effect**, after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who worked out its mathematics in 1835. Nothing is pushing the air: it is how a straight path looks from a turning Earth. It is strongest near the poles, nothing at the equator, and far too weak to decide which way a sink drains.

front-name.title: Why “front”?
front-name.text: The word comes from a group of weather scientists in Bergen, Norway, led by Vilhelm Bjerknes and his son Jacob, just after the First World War. They pictured the boundary between cold and warm air as a battle line, where two armies of air met and pushed each other back and forth, and borrowed the soldiers’ word for it.

puy-de-dome.title: A barometer up a mountain
puy-de-dome.text: If the air really holds the mercury up, there should be less air to do it on a mountain. In 1648 Blaise Pascal had his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, carry a mercury tube up the Puy de Dôme, an old volcano in central France, while a second tube stayed in the town below. At the top, about a kilometre higher, the mercury stood some 8 centimetres lower.
